oneLiner: A four-week Launch Readiness Diagnostic that tests PlayBlue's four stated differentiators, ranks category demand, and maps the price corridor against Decathlon — in the last window where the answers can still change the store.

whyNow.title: The window is closing
whyNow.text: Assortment, pricing, floor plan and staffing model are being decided in the next few months. After the Bengaluru opening, the same research measures a decision already made and paid for. This is the only period where the findings are cheap to act on.

whyNow.title: The cost asymmetry is extreme
whyNow.text: A wrong assortment call on a 15,000 sq ft store, or a permanent staffing line for a differentiator customers do not value, runs into crores over a store's life — and repeats at every subsequent store. The diagnostic is a fraction of one store's fit-out.

whyNow.title: It produces the Series A evidence base
whyNow.text: Centre Court's thesis is explicitly analytics-weighted. A consumer dataset PlayBlue owns — bottom-up sizing, willingness-to-pay, segment preference — is exactly the material that makes a profitability case checkable rather than asserted.

whyNow.title: Nothing comparable exists
whyNow.text: There is no public India-specific evidence on whether consumers will pay for multi-brand curation in sport. Whoever runs it first owns the answer — and it is a defensible asset going into brand negotiations as well as investor conversations.

modules.title: Differentiator & positioning test
modules.question: Do PlayBlue's four stated differentiators actually drive preference against the real competitive set — and which one carries the most weight per rupee it costs to deliver?
modules.how: Scored consumer panel in Bengaluru and Mumbai, running the PlayBlue proposition head-to-head against Decathlon, marketplaces, single-brand D2C and vertically integrated challengers. Attributes scored individually, then trade-off tested so we learn relative weight rather than just approval.

attrs.label: Trust in curation
attrs.value: Does "we chose these 100 brands for you" reduce or increase decision anxiety?

attrs.label: Value of expert guidance
attrs.value: Is staffed advice a reason to visit, or perceived sales pressure?

attrs.label: Delivery speed
attrs.value: Willingness to pay for 4-hour against next-day and click-and-collect

attrs.label: Community & membership
attrs.value: Would they join one, and what would have to be in it?

attrs.label: Price perception
attrs.value: Where PlayBlue is placed relative to the Decathlon anchor before any price is shown

attrs.label: Channel preference
attrs.value: Store versus online by category — which categories need to be touched

kv.label: Sample
kv.value: n ≈ 600, screened for category purchase in last 12 months, quota'd on income band and activity level

kv.label: Output
kv.value: Attribute scorecard by segment, relative-weight ranking, verbatim consumer language, positioning recommendation

kv.label: Decision it de-risks
kv.value: Staffing model, delivery investment, brand messaging, store comms

modules.title: Category & assortment demand ranking
modules.question: Across six categories and 100+ brands, which combinations actually pull demand — and which are shelf space spent on optics?
modules.how: MaxDiff trade-off exercise across sport categories and a brand-preference screen within each. Cross-cut by the four consumer groups in the plan, plus the parent-buying-for-child segment MIXI flagged and PlayBlue has not named. Includes an explicit white-space read: categories consumers want organised retail for and cannot currently find.

kv.label: Output
kv.value: Ranked category architecture, brand priority tiers, white-space list, segment-by-category demand matrix

kv.label: Decision it de-risks
kv.value: Buying plan, space allocation, brand partnership sequencing

modules.title: Price corridor mapping
modules.question: In which categories can a curated multi-brand format hold a premium, and where does the ₹399 Decathlon t-shirt make a premium unsellable?
modules.how: Van Westendorp price sensitivity by category, plus a competitive price audit across Decathlon, marketplace listings and brand D2C on matched products. Produces acceptable price bands rather than a single point.

kv.label: Output
kv.value: Acceptable price band by category, premium-defensible list, categories where PlayBlue must match or exit

kv.label: Decision it de-risks
kv.value: Margin planning, promotional policy, the private-label question

timeline.title: Scoping session
timeline.text: Half a day with your team. We align on the competitive set to test against, the categories to cover, and the specific decisions the output has to serve. You approve the instrument before anything goes to field.

timeline.title: Instrument design and pilot
timeline.text: Questionnaire built and soft-launched to a small cell to check comprehension and screen-out rates. Leading or biased questions flagged and corrected before full field.

timeline.title: Fielding
timeline.text: Full panel in Bengaluru and Mumbai. Live progress visibility — you see completion by city, segment and quota as it fills, not at the end.

timeline.title: Analysis and interim readout
timeline.text: Cleaning, de-duplication, open-end coding, cross-tabs. A 30-minute interim call on headline findings so nothing in the final report is a surprise, and so you can redirect the cut if something unexpected appears.

timeline.title: Delivery and working session
timeline.text: Decision brief plus the underlying data. We walk the team through it and stay for the argument — the output is meant to be challenged, not filed.

whatYouGet.title: A decision brief, not a deck
whatYouGet.text: Headline finding, the evidence under it, and a recommended action per decision. Structured so a section can be lifted straight into a board pack.

whatYouGet.title: The raw data
whatYouGet.text: Full response set, coded open-ends, cross-tab tables. Yours to keep, re-cut and re-run. We are not building a dependency.

whatYouGet.title: A re-runnable instrument
whatYouGet.text: The same questionnaire can be fielded again post-launch to measure movement. Wave one becomes a baseline rather than a one-off.

whatYouGet.title: Consumer language
whatYouGet.text: Verbatims in the words customers actually use — directly usable in store signage, product copy and staff training.

needVsNot.title: What we need
needVsNot.text: Half a day for scoping. The competitive set you actually consider yourself against. Your current category list and any indicative price architecture. One named decision-owner. That is the whole ask.

needVsNot.title: What this does not do
needVsNot.text: It will not select your sites — that is a separate study with a spatial component. It will not tell you what your unit economics are, because that needs your cost data. It will not validate the 4-hour delivery build economically; it only tells you what customers will pay for it.

judgeCallout: Three tests, agreed upfront. One: at least one differentiator is ranked materially lower by consumers than PlayBlue currently assumes, or all four are confirmed with evidence you can cite. Two: the category ranking changes at least one buying decision. Three: you can state a price position by category with a number behind it. If none of those happen, the study did not earn its cost and we would rather you knew the criteria in advance.
stagingCallout: If a four-week scope is too much for a first engagement, Module A alone runs in two to three weeks and answers the highest-value question on its own. We would rather start narrow and earn the rest than oversell the first piece.
